title: Flagship fest ahead, why Nagaland wants permit regime scrapped
syllabus: GS3 › Security challenges and their management in border areas; Linkages of development and security · GS2 › Federalism and Centre–state relations; Issues relating to the Northeast · GS1 › Tribal culture · GS4 › Citizen-friendly administration
summary: Nagaland has urged the Centre to completely withdraw the Protected Area Permit for foreigners, reimposed in December 2024 for security reasons, saying it hurts tourism ahead of the Hornbill Festival.
ideas: Two permits, two purposes: the PAP (Foreigners (Protected Areas) Order, 1958) controls foreigners' entry to border states, while the colonial-era ILP regulates Indian citizens to protect indigenous hill cultures.
GS3 · Border management / GS1 · Tribal culture
India's permit regimes serve two aims: security at the border (PAP) and protection of tribal cultures (ILP).
Security versus development: relaxed in 2011 and reimposed in December 2024 for security reasons, the PAP now clashes with the state's push for tourism and investment.
GS3 · Linkages of security and development
In peaceful border states, rigid security rules can choke the development that itself secures the region.
A rule from another era: the CM argues that a regulation designed for a different security environment should not hold back a peaceful state's aspirations.
Rules must be reviewed as conditions change; regulations that outlive their purpose become obstacles.
Process matters as much as policy: bureaucracy, a convoluted application process and last-minute relaxations deter foreign tourists who plan months ahead.
Predictable, simple procedures matter as much as the rule itself for tourism and trust.
Federal voice: the state wants a central rule changed and has taken it to the Union Home Minister, but awaits a decision.
Nagaland's appeal on the PAP shows states seeking a voice in central rules that shape their development.
